Definition 1. A function G: Rr → R† is an equidistant function if its graph is the equidistant set of K and I for a positive-valued continuous function J. Lemma 3. The equidistant function G: Rr → Rt belonging to a positive-valued continuous function f: Rr → Rt is continuous. Proof. Taking In → x, the sequence Yr = G(xn) is obviously bounded because of the continuity of the function f: for all but finitely many indices, O<Yn =G(Xn) < f(Xn) < f(x) +E. Therefore it has a convergent subsequence. Since the distance-measuring functions d((x, y), L) and d((x, y), K) are continuous, it can easily be seen that any convergent subsequence of n gives a subsequence of (Xn, Yn) tending to a point (x, y) such that d((x, y), L) = d((x, y), K). The unicity of the equidistant point at x implies that y = G(x) is the common limit of the convergent subsequences of Yn = G(xn). Therefore Yn = G(xn) → y = G(x). Theorem 1. Then there exists at least one index i € 1 such that y > Gi(x) and Lemma 2 implies that d((x, y), Li) < d((x, y), K). Since L:= epi fmin = Vier epi fi = Vier Li, we have d((x, Y), L) = d((x, Y), ViI Li) ≤ d((x, Y), Li) < d((x, Y), K) and Lemma 2 implies that y > Gmin (x). On the other hand, suppose that y < min{Gi(x) | i E!}. Then y < Gi(x) for all i € I and Lemma 2 implies that d((x, y), K) < d((x, y), Li) for all i € I. Thus

d((x, Y), K) < min{d((x, y), Li) | i E 1} = d((x, y), ViI Li) = d((x, y), L)
